title: Knees and bows
hookLine: the knee bends toward the tabernacle; the head bows at the name of Jesus

cards: Before a Catholic slides into a pew, something odd happens. They stop in the aisle, face the front, and drop down on one knee. Just for a second, then up again, and in they go.

If you didn't grow up with it, it can look like someone about to propose, or tie a shoe. Later in the Mass, a whole church bows its heads at the same moment, like wheat in the wind. Nobody announced it.
Everyone just knew. In this part of Camp Three the body prays, and today it does it without a word.

teach.b: Genuflect comes from two Latin words: genu, knee, and flectere, to bend. It's an old sign of honor.
At Mass, Catholics do it toward one thing: the tabernacle, the small locked cabinet where the consecrated bread from Mass is kept. Catholics believe that bread is Christ himself, really present.
So a lamp, often red, burns near the tabernacle day and night, and the right knee goes down to the floor in front of it, the way you'd greet someone you love and honor.
If a church keeps the tabernacle in a side chapel, people bow to the altar instead. Then there's the head.

teach.h: A BOW AT THE NAME OF JESUS.
teach.b: Catholics are asked to bow their heads at the name of Jesus, and at the names of Mary and the saint of the day.
Once each Sunday, in the Creed, at the words about Jesus being born of the Virgin Mary and becoming man, everyone is asked to bow.

teach.h: WHAT THE BODY CAN, NOT MORE.
teach.b: At Christmas and on the feast of the Annunciation, they kneel for those words instead. Paul has a line for this, written long before there were church buildings.

teach.h: THAT IN THE NAME OF JESUS EVERY KNEE SHOULD BOW.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow." People who can't kneel bow instead, and Catholics count that just as much a prayer. Eastern Catholics have their own tradition of deep bows.
Catholics would put it this way: before the words come, before you've had a chance to think, the body has already said what it believes.

how: Catholics genuflect on the right knee toward the tabernacle when entering or leaving a pew, bow their heads at the name of Jesus, and bow at the words of the incarnation in the Creed; those who cannot kneel make a bow instead.

games.q: it's an ordinary Sunday. the Creed reaches the words about Jesus being born of the Virgin Mary and becoming man. what does the church do?
games.why: everyone bows. only at Christmas and on the feast of the Annunciation do they kneel for those words.

practice: Sit up straight, then slowly lower your head: not a nod, a real bow that takes three seconds going down, and hold it, noticing how it feels to lower yourself on purpose with nobody watching. If you pray, bow toward God.
If not, bow toward whatever in your life deserves it, someone's kindness, a gift you didn't earn, and then rise.

wordCard.voice: Genuflect. To bend the knee, the way Catholics greet Christ present in the tabernacle.

orig.note: Latin: to bend the knee, the root of genuflect.

carryVoice: Your line: the body says it first. Crossed arms, a turned back, a leaning in: posture speaks before words do. See you tomorrow.
